land.text: the Ming south of the Yangtze and the Huai ('south of the Huai and Yangtze rivers', named only in passing on the Southern Ming page), under the Prince of Fu

predecessors.note: 'The Prince of Fu was crowned as the Hongguang emperor on June 19' 1644; the infobox calls the state a 'Rump state of the Ming dynasty'. Cliopatria starts the row in 1645.

land.text: Yunnan and the south-west, taken by the Qing in 1658-59, and the Yongli Emperor, handed over in Burma on 22 January 1662

successors.note: The qing-dynasty dossier (ea-08) records the Southern Ming provinces as its gains of 1645-1659.

land.text: Taiwan, where Koxinga's Kingdom of Tungning claimed 'to be the rightful Ming successor until 1683'

successors.note: The Southern Ming page lists Tungning as a successor; Cliopatria draws Taiwan as 'Southern Ming' in 1662-1672 (shape southern-ming_1662), which belongs to the Tungning dossier.

capitals.name: Fuzhou (Tianxing)
capitals.note: Infobox 'Tianxing (1645-1646)'; the Longwu court at Fuzhou, enthroned 18 August 1645.

capitals.name: Zhaoqing
capitals.note: Infobox lists Guangzhou (1646, the Shaowu court of 11 December) and Zhaoqing (1646); Yongli ascended in Zhaoqing, 24 December 1646.

capitals.name: Nanning
capitals.note: After Guangzhou fell on 20 January 1647 the Yongli Emperor fled to Nanning; the Qing conquest page's infobox has 'Nanning court (1646-1662)'. The court also stopped at Guilin and in Guizhou in 1649-50 without a dated seat.

capitals.name: Anlong (Guizhou)
capitals.note: 'The Yongli court is at Anlong (1652-1659)'. Coordinates are approximate (the gazetteer has no Anlong).

capitals.name: Kunming (Yunnanfu)
capitals.note: 'In 1658 Zhu Youlang retreated to Kunming in Yunnan.' The Southern Ming page: a Qing army took the Yunnan capital in late January 1659.

capitals.name: Ava (Burma), the court in exile
capitals.note: The Yongli Emperor sought refuge under King Pindale Min; handed over on 22 January 1662. Coordinates approximate; the page names no town.

rulers.name: Shaowu (Zhu Yuyue)
rulers.note: 11 December 1646 - 20 January 1647; a rival court at Guangzhou

correction.text: The Hongguang court's realm of June 1644 to June 1645, taken from Cliopatria's 1645 shape: the Ming south of the Huai and the Yangtze

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria begins the row in 1645 but 'The Prince of Fu was crowned as the Hongguang emperor on June 19' 1644 at Nanjing. The page gives no boundary ('south of the Huai and Yangtze rivers' in passing), so Cliopatria's 1645 shape is used as the claimed realm.

correction.text: Cliopatria's 1645 shape without Jiangsu (Nanjing, June 1645), Zhejiang (February 1646) and Fujian (October 1646), as it stands from 1646

keyframe_review.note: 2.18 M km2, Jiangsu to Yunnan. Right for the Hongguang year (to 15 June 1645), too large afterwards: Nanjing surrendered on 8 June 1645, the Qing took 'land west of the Qiantang River from the Lu regime' in February 1646, Fuzhou on 17 October 1646 and Guangzhou on 20 January 1647. The Southern Ming page gives no area to check against. The corrected shape holds from 1646; the ledger carries the steps.

correction.text: Cliopatria's 1648 shape without Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Fujian, which were Qing since 1645-46

keyframe_review.note: 2.17 M km2 for 1648-1652 still holds Jiangsu (63 per cent), Zhejiang and Fujian, which the Qing had taken in 1645-46. What the Southern Ming held in 1648-52 is Guangdong (until the Qing retook it in 1649-50 and Guangzhou on 24 November 1650: 'May 1648: Li Chengdong mutinies against the Qing'), Guangxi, Guizhou and Yunnan, with Huguang and Jiangxi until 1649-50.

correction.text: Guangxi (Guilin, August 1652), Guizhou (the court at Anlong, 1652-1659) and Yunnan, to the Qing campaign of late 1658 and the fall of the Yunnan capital in late January 1659

keyframe_review.note: 198,795 km2 (about half of Yunnan) for 1653-1658. The Southern Ming page has the court at Anlong (1652-1659), Guilin retaken by Li Dingguo in August 1652 and, in 1658, 'Qing forces launch a multipronged campaign against Guizhou and Yunnan': so the realm of these years is Guangxi, Guizhou and Yunnan, not half of Yunnan. Li Dingguo had served under Zhang Xianzhong; the Xi remnants held Yunnan and Guizhou (Zhang Xianzhong page).

correction.text: Shape unchanged; the years 1662-1672 belong to the Kingdom of Tungning (kingdom-of-tungning), not to the Southern Ming

keyframe_review.note: 40,939 km2 of Taiwan for 1662-1672. The Southern Ming page ends the Yongli Emperor's reign in 1662 (captured in Burma 22 January, strangled in June) and has Koxinga establish the Kingdom of Tungning on Taiwan; the 'Prince of Ningjing, in Tungning, claims to be the rightful Ming successor until 1683, though he lacks real power'. The island belongs to the kingdom-of-tungning dossier (1661-1683), whose shape is the western plain only.

correction.text: Shape unchanged; the years 1673-1676 belong to Wu Sangui's rebellion (wu-sangui-s-zhou) and, for Taiwan, to the Kingdom of Tungning

keyframe_review.note: 976,185 km2 (Yunnan, Guangdong, Guangxi, Fujian, Taiwan) for 1673-1676 is the Revolt of the Three Feudatories (infobox 'August 1673 - November 1681'): Wu Sangui's rising from December 1673, Fujian under Geng Jingzhong and Guangxi under Sun Yanling in 1674, Guangdong under Shang Zhixin in 1676, with Tungning landing in Fujian and Guangdong in 1674. None of it is Southern Ming. See wu-sangui-s-zhou.

correction.text: Shape unchanged; the years 1677-1682 belong to Wu Sangui's Zhou (wu-sangui-s-zhou) and to the Kingdom of Tungning

keyframe_review.note: 1.93 M km2 for 1677-1682, the Three Feudatories at their widest (Hunan, Sichuan and Guizhou added: 'captured Hunan and Sichuan provinces'); Wu Sangui 'proclaimed himself emperor of the Great Zhou Dynasty' at Hengzhou in 1678 and died that year, and the Qing recovered the provinces in 1678-1681. Not Southern Ming. See wu-sangui-s-zhou.

ledger.note: 1644: Ryukyu pays tribute to the Southern Ming. Infobox 'Tributary state of the Southern Ming (1644-1646)'; the Ryukyu page's body text is silent.

region.text: Nanjing and the south of the Huai and the Yangtze

ledger.note: 1644: the Prince of Fu is crowned Hongguang Emperor at Nanjing. 'The Prince of Fu was crowned as the Hongguang emperor on June 19.' The page names no boundary: the realm is Cliopatria's 1645 shape.
1645: Nanjing surrenders to the Qing without a fight (8 June; the page also gives 6 June); the Hongguang Emperor is captured on 15 June. The Prince of Lu is regent in Zhejiang from October.
1645: the Longwu court at Fuzhou. The Prince of Tang 'declares himself regent', takes the title on 29 July and is enthroned on 18 August; infobox Tianxing (1645-1646).

1646: the end of Ryukyu's Southern Ming tribute. The infobox reads 'Tributary state of the Southern Ming (1644-1646)'; the body text is silent on the break, so the year is the infobox's and nothing is redrawn.

region.text: Zhejiang west of the Qiantang River

ledger.note: 1646: Qing forces take land west of the Qiantang River. 'Qing forces take land west of the Qiantang River from the Lu regime and defeat Longwu forces in northeastern Jiangxi' (February).
1646: Fuzhou falls. The Longwu Emperor was executed at Tingzhou on 6 October; 'Fuzhou falls' on 17 October and Zheng Zhilong defects, 'but Koxinga keeps resisting'.
1646: the Yongli Emperor ascends at Zhaoqing. Zhu Youlang 'establishes the Yongli regime' on 24 December 1646, thirteen days after the Shaowu court was proclaimed in Guangzhou (11 December).

region.text: Guangzhou and the Pearl River delta

ledger.note: 1647: Guangzhou falls. 'Li Chengdong ... captures Guangzhou' on 20 January 1647, the Shaowu Emperor kills himself and the Yongli Emperor flees to Nanning.
1647: the court at Nanning. The Yongli Emperor 'flees to Nanning'; the Qing conquest page gives 'Nanning court (1646-1662)'.
1648: Guangdong returns. 'Li Chengdong mutinies against the Qing' in May 1648, the Qing governor of Guangdong declaring for the Ming.

1649: Huguang and Jiangxi are retaken. '1649-1650: Qing forces retake Huguang, Jiangxi, and Guangdong'; the Yongli Emperor 'flees to Nanning and then Guizhou'. The page gives the span, so the year is the first.
1650: Guangzhou falls again. 'Shang Kexi captures Guangzhou after a ten-month siege and massacres its population' on 24 November 1650.
1652: Li Dingguo retakes Guilin. 'Li Dingguo, who had served under Zhang Xianzhong ... retakes Guilin' in early August 1652 and 'Most Qing-aligned commanders in Guangxi switch sides within a month'.
1652: the court at Anlong. 'The Yongli court is at Anlong (1652-1659).'
1658: the court retreats to Kunming. 'In 1658 Zhu Youlang retreated to Kunming in Yunnan.'

1658: the Qing attack Guizhou and Yunnan. 'Qing forces launch a multipronged campaign against Guizhou and Yunnan' in late 1658; Hong Chengchou had been put 'in charge of retaking the southwest' in 1653.
1659: the Qing take the Yunnan capital in late January and the Yongli Emperor flees to Burma. A Qing army under Doni takes the city.
1659: Yunnan falls. 'A Qing army under Doni takes the Yunnan capital' in late January 1659.

1659: Guizhou and Guangxi pass to the Qing, bridging. The 1658 campaign was 'against Guizhou and Yunnan'; the Qing dossier's Cliopatria shape has both provinces Qing in 1659; the page is silent on Guangxi.

1659: the court in exile in Burma. The Southern Ming page: the Yongli Emperor 'flees into Burma, then ruled by King Pindale Min' (late January 1659); the Yongli page says 'He finally fled into Burma in 1661' (the court had taken refuge under Pindale Min earlier). The two pages disagree; the Cliopatria shape ends in 1658.

region.text: the Yongli court at Ava, Burma

ledger.note: 1661: the Qing demand the emperor. 'A Qing army of 20,000 under Wu Sangui entered Burma and demanded the surrender of Youlang' in December 1661, after Pye Min overthrew his brother in May.

region.text: the last Cliopatria shape of the Southern Ming proper (Yunnan); the court was in Burma and then Kunming

ledger.note: 1662: the Yongli Emperor is executed and the Southern Ming end. 'On 22 January 1662, the last monarch of the Southern Ming, together with his sons and grandsons, were put on boats'; 'Wu Sangui captures and executes the Yongli Emperor' in June at Kunming. Taiwan's Tungning keeps the Ming claim to 1683.

wars.name: Qing conquest of the Southern Ming: Nanjing and Fujian
wars.outcome: Nanjing surrendered on 8 June 1645, the Hongguang Emperor was captured on 15 June, Qing forces took land west of the Qiantang in February 1646 and Fuzhou on 17 October 1646; the Longwu Emperor was executed on 6 October.

wars.name: Qing conquest of the Southern Ming: Guangdong and Guangxi
wars.outcome: Guangzhou fell on 20 January 1647 and again on 24 November 1650 after Li Chengdong's mutiny of May 1648; Huguang and Jiangxi were retaken in 1649-50; Li Dingguo retook Guilin in August 1652.

wars.name: Qing conquest of the south-west
wars.outcome: A multipronged Qing campaign in late 1658 took the Yunnan capital in late January 1659; the Yongli Emperor, in Burma, was handed over on 22 January 1662 and strangled in June.
wars.note: The Qing conquest page lists the courts: Nanjing (1644-45), Fuzhou (1645-46), Guangzhou (1646-47), Nanning (1646-62).

certainty.note: No page gives a boundary: the Southern Ming's land is the part of the south its courts held at the time, changing with the Qing columns.

notes:
Written by ea-07 on 2026-10-25 from the eight pages in sources (page budget up to 5 for six shapes; the Southern Ming, Yongli Emperor and Three Feudatories pages are the core, the Qing-conquest and Ming pages are shared with ming-dynasty). Quotes in notes are as WebFetch returned them.

Cliopatria row to split. 'Southern Ming' runs 1645-1682 in six shapes. The Southern Ming proper is 1644-1662: the Yongli Emperor was strangled in June 1662 (Southern Ming and Yongli pages; the Ming page's infobox 'End of the Southern Ming: 1662'). (1) southern-ming_1662 (Taiwan, 1662-1672, 40,939 km2) is the Kingdom of Tungning, already written by ea-08-x as kingdom-of-tungning (1661-1683, whose own shape is the western plain only; Cliopatria's whole-island patch is the better one for the island). (2) southern-ming_1673 and southern-ming_1677 (976,185 and 1.93 M km2) are Wu Sangui's rebellion of the Three Feudatories, dossier wu-sangui-s-zhou (written by ea-07), with Taiwan again Tungning's. The qing-dynasty dossier (ea-08) records the 1673-1681 losses against southern-ming; they should read wu-sangui-s-zhou. The shapes of 1645 and 1648 hold the whole south, including Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Fujian that the Qing had taken in 1645-46: corrected (adjust).

Not settled: the Hongguang realm's extent (the page says only 'south of the Huai and Yangtze rivers'); the Prince of Lu's Zhejiang regime (regent from October 1645, not a dossier; Zhoushan is not on the page); the Shaowu court at Guangzhou (41 days, 11 December 1646 - 20 January 1647, ruler listed, no seat of its own); Sun Kewang, Li Dingguo and the Xi remnants' alliance with the Southern Ming (the Southern Ming page does not mention an alliance; Li Dingguo 'had served under Zhang Xianzhong'), so Guizhou and Yunnan in 1648-58 may be partly Xi remnant land; the Southern Ming has no land between January 1659 and June 1662 (a court in Burma). Page disagreements: Nanjing surrendered on 6 or 8 June 1645 (one page); Yongli fled into Burma in January 1659 (Southern Ming page, and the Qing dossier) or 1661 (Yongli page); Yongli's enthronement is November or 24 December 1646 (Yongli page); the Southern Ming page confuses the Prince of Lu's regent (Zhu Changfang or Zhu Yihai). The gazetteer lacks Anlong and Ava (capitals use coordinates). The Ryukyu dossier has the Southern Ming tribute 1644-1646, matched here.
